# Stage 7 - Out-of-sample validation {#stage7}

Feeds article 2.7 and 3.7.

Everything above is apparent performance, scored on the data it was
fitted to, which is optimistic by construction. `r length(coef(m3))`
covariates is ample opportunity to fit noise. Two hold-outs, chosen
because they fail differently:

-   Temporal split: train 2021-22 to 2024-25, test 2025-26. The
    operational question, and how a rolling tool would actually run.
-   Player-grouped 5-fold CV: whole players held out. A random row split
    would put LeBron's game 5 in training and game 6 in test, so the
    model could score well by memorising him.

Two safeguards: z-scores computed on training rows only, otherwise the
test distribution leaks into training; and `strata(SEASON)` dropped,
because a stratified model has no baseline for a season it never saw and
discrimination needs only the linear predictor.

```{r validation-setup, dependson="model-specs"}
zcols <- c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ACWR_MIN","ROLLING_GAMES_7D",
           "ROLLING_DIST_7D","ROLLING_DIST_28D","SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST","MIN",
           "PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN",
           "ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ACWR_LOAD",
           "PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",
           "PREV_GAME_INTENSITY","PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY",
           "ROLLING_B2B_7D","ROLLING_B2B_28D","PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER",
           "TEAM_DAYS_REST","SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE","CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",
           "PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON","PCT_THROUGH_SEASON","HEIGHT_INCHES","WEIGHT")

# primary = the reported load model; minutes = the same spec with minutes swapped in,
# validated out of sample as the robustness check (both on the new-injury outcome).
specs <- list(
  primary = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added)),
  minutes = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added))
)

# Standardise using TRAIN mean/sd only, then apply that same scaling to test.
add_z <- function(train, test, cols) {
  for (cc in cols) {
    m <- mean(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE); s <- sd(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE)
    train[[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (train[[cc]] - m) / s
    test [[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (test [[cc]] - m) / s
  }
  list(train = train, test = test)
}

# No season strata, so the risk score transfers to unseen seasons/players.
fit_spec <- function(data, spec) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", spec$outcome, ") ~ ",
                          paste(spec$terms, collapse = " + "), " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")),
        data = data, ties = "efron")
}

# concordance(Surv ~ x) treats larger x as LONGER survival; a Cox risk score is the
# opposite, so reverse = TRUE flips it back to the conventional C-index.
c_index <- function(fit, data, outcome) {
  d <- data
  d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = data, type = "lp"))
  concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
              data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance
}
```

```{r temporal-validation, dependson="validation-setup"}
test_season <- "2025-26"
tr0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON != test_season)
te0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == test_season)

temporal <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  sc  <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
  fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
  tibble(model      = nm,
         apparent_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$train, sp$outcome), 4),
         temporal_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$test,  sp$outcome), 4))
})

show_tbl(temporal, paste0("Temporal validation - trained pre-", test_season,
                          ", tested on ", test_season))
```

```{r oos-calibration, dependson="temporal-validation"}
sc    <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
fit_p <- fit_spec(sc$train, specs$primary)

calib_oos <- sc$test %>%
  mutate(risk = as.numeric(predict(fit_p, newdata = ., type = "lp"))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(risk)) %>%
  mutate(risk_group = ntile(risk, 5)) %>%      # 5 bands, not 10 - the test season is smaller
  group_by(risk_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), events = sum(event),
            event_rate_1k = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 1), .groups = "drop")

show_tbl(calib_oos, "Out-of-sample calibration in the held-out season (primary model)")
```

```{r player-cv, dependson="validation-setup"}
set.seed(42)
players <- tibble(PLAYER_ID = unique(cox$PLAYER_ID),
                  fold      = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID))))
coxf <- cox %>% left_join(players, by = "PLAYER_ID")

player_cv <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  oos <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(coxf))          # every row gets a score from a model blind to it
  for (k in 1:5) {
    tr  <- coxf %>% filter(fold != k)       # the other four folds' players
    idx <- which(coxf$fold == k)
    sc  <- add_z(tr, coxf[idx, ], zcols)
    fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
    oos[idx] <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = sc$test, type = "lp"))
  }
  d <- coxf; d$.lp <- oos
  tibble(model = nm,
         player_cv_C = round(
           concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", sp$outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
                       data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance, 4))
})

validation_summary <- temporal %>% left_join(player_cv, by = "model")
show_tbl(validation_summary, "Validation summary - apparent vs two out-of-sample estimates")
```

## What it shows

The out-of-sample estimates land essentially on top of the apparent one.
The largest drop under either scheme is
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(validation_summary$apparent_C - validation_summary$temporal_C, validation_summary$apparent_C - validation_summary$player_cv_C))`
of concordance, and on the temporal split the held-out season actually
scores marginally higher than the training data. There is no detectable
optimism here: apparent performance is what this model would deliver on
data it has never seen. Both schemes agreeing matters, since the
temporal split would expose a model that only worked in its training
seasons and the player-grouped CV would expose one that had memorised
players.

The minutes spec lands on top of the load model out of sample, so the
exposure choice makes no difference to generalisation. Out-of-sample
calibration holds too: injury rates still climb across risk bands built
from the frozen model. The ranking transfers.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 8 - Rolling risk profiles {#stage8}

Feeds article 3.7, Figure 4 and Tables 8-9. The applied deliverable.

Model 3's linear predictor is a per-player-per-game risk score, the same
quantity calibrated in Stage 3. Plotted over a season it becomes a
trajectory. To make it read as relative rather than an uninterpretable
log-hazard, I overlay the league median and IQR at each game number.
Above the band means more modelled risk than a typical player at that
point; the shape shows when.

I plot 2025-26 using Model 3, which is fitted on all five seasons, so
these profiles are **in-sample illustrations** of the ranking, not
prospective scores. The genuinely held-out evidence is the temporal
validation in Stage 7, which trains without 2025-26. Three exemplars:
LeBron James as the familiar anchor, one player the model rates well
above the league, and one who played a full season with no injury
episodes. The test is conceptual: does each profile match what we
independently know about that player's durability and availability?

```{r risk-profiles, dependson="m3", fig.height=8.5, fig.width=8}
TEST <- "2025-26"
attr(m3$terms, ".Environment") <- environment()   # see the note in the calibration chunk
cox$risk_lp <- as.numeric(predict(m3, newdata = cox, type = "lp"))
season <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == TEST, !is.na(risk_lp))

# League band: median + IQR of the risk score across everyone at each game number.
band <- season %>% group_by(game = t_stop) %>%
  summarise(q1 = quantile(risk_lp, .25), med = median(risk_lp),
            q3 = quantile(risk_lp, .75), .groups = "drop")

# Three exemplars chosen to span the risk range (see text).
# Player-level check FIRST, so the three exemplars illustrate a relationship rather
# than standing in for one. Mean risk score per player against their injury count.
player_lvl <- season %>%
  left_join(band %>% select(t_stop = game, med), by = "t_stop") %>%
  group_by(PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  summarise(intervals = n(), played = sum(PLAYED_FLAG), events = sum(event),
            missed = max(SEASON_GAMES_MISSED),
            mean_lp = mean(risk_lp), pct_above = mean(risk_lp > med), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(intervals >= 40)

rho_missed <- cor(player_lvl$mean_lp, player_lvl$missed, method = "spearman")

quint_tab <- player_lvl %>%
  mutate(q = ntile(mean_lp, 5)) %>%
  group_by(`Risk quintile` = q) %>%
  summarise(Players = n(),
            `Mean games played` = round(mean(played), 1),
            `Total injury events` = sum(events),
            `Injury events per player` = round(mean(events), 2), .groups = "drop")
rho_events <- cor(player_lvl$mean_lp, player_lvl$events, method = "spearman")
show_tbl(quint_tab, paste0("Player-level risk score against injury count, ", TEST,
                           ", in-sample (Spearman rho = ", round(rho_events, 2), ")"))

# Three exemplars. Chosen on injury EVENTS, not games missed - see the note below on why
# games missed is the wrong target.
# Every label is read off the data rather than typed in. Hand-written labels went stale
# twice: once claiming five episodes for Johnson while the tables said seven, and once
# calling Shead "lowest risk" after the timing fix had moved him onto the league median.
pick_names <- c("Jalen Johnson", "LeBron James", "Jamal Shead")
picks <- player_lvl %>% filter(PLAYER_NAME %in% pick_names) %>%
  transmute(PLAYER_NAME,
            role = paste0(if_else(events == 0, "no injury episodes",
                                  paste0(events, " injury episode", if_else(events == 1, "", "s"))),
                          "; above the league median in ", round(100 * pct_above),
                          "% of games")) %>%
  slice(match(pick_names, PLAYER_NAME))

ex <- season %>% inner_join(picks, by = "PLAYER_NAME") %>%
  arrange(PLAYER_NAME, t_stop) %>% group_by(PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  mutate(seg = cumsum(c(1, as.integer(diff(t_stop) > 3)))) %>%  # break the line across absence spells
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(facet = factor(paste0(PLAYER_NAME, "\n", role),
                        levels = paste0(picks$PLAYER_NAME, "\n", picks$role)))
band_f <- tidyr::crossing(facet = levels(ex$facet), band) %>%
  mutate(facet = factor(facet, levels = levels(ex$facet)))
events <- ex %>% filter(event == 1)

# Quantitative check: does the profile match availability + injuries?
prof_tab <- season %>% inner_join(picks, by = "PLAYER_NAME") %>%
  left_join(band %>% select(t_stop = game, med), by = "t_stop") %>%
  group_by(Player = PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  summarise(`Games played`  = sum(PLAYED_FLAG),
            `Injury events` = sum(event),
            `Mean risk score` = round(mean(risk_lp), 2),
            `% games above league median` = round(100 * mean(risk_lp > med)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(`Mean risk score`))
get_stat <- function(nm, col) prof_tab[[col]][prof_tab$Player == nm]
show_tbl(prof_tab, paste0("Exemplar risk profiles vs actual availability, ", TEST, ", in-sample"))

fig_profiles <- ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = band_f, aes(game, ymin = q1, ymax = q3), fill = "grey80", alpha = .6) +
  geom_line(data = band_f, aes(game, med), colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(data = ex, aes(t_stop, risk_lp, group = seg, colour = facet), linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(data = ex, aes(t_stop, risk_lp, colour = facet), size = .9) +
  geom_point(data = events, aes(t_stop, risk_lp), shape = 4, size = 3, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ facet, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#2166ac", "#1a9850"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = paste0("Rolling injury-risk profiles, ", TEST, " (in-sample)"),
       subtitle = paste0("Model 3 risk score by game; Model 3 is fitted on all five seasons.\n",
                         "Grey = league IQR, dashed = league median, red x = injury onset."),
       x = "Game number within season", y = "Risk score (Model 3 linear predictor)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
fig_profiles
```

## What it shows

The quintile table is the general claim: player-level mean risk score
orders injury count across the season (Spearman rho =
`r round(rho_events, 2)`), so the three profiles illustrate a real
relationship rather than standing in for one.

Jalen Johnson sits above the league median in
`r get_stat("Jalen Johnson", "% games above league median")`% of his
games with `r get_stat("Jalen Johnson", "Injury events")` onsets, the
season's highest burden. LeBron James is above the median in
`r get_stat("LeBron James", "% games above league median")`% of games
with `r get_stat("LeBron James", "Injury events")` onsets. Jamal Shead
played `r get_stat("Jamal Shead", "Games played")` games with
`r get_stat("Jamal Shead", "Injury events")` onsets and sits around the
league median (above it in
`r get_stat("Jamal Shead", "% games above league median")`% of games).
At concordance `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 2)`, about
`r round(100 * (1 - summary(m3)$concordance[1]))`% of comparable pairs
are ordered wrongly, so a three-player figure has no right to be immune.

A note on what these profiles are scored against. The instinct is to
validate against games missed, and that is the wrong target. Across the
`r nrow(player_lvl)` players with 40+ modelled intervals in `r TEST`,
mean risk score correlates with games missed at Spearman
`r round(rho_missed, 2)`, negative: higher-scoring players miss fewer
games, because a high score requires high load and high load requires
being available. Games missed mixes injury with rest, load management
and coaching decisions. Onsets are what the model is fitted to.

Two caveats. The score is relative, so it ranks but gives no absolute
probability. And Shead, injury-free across a full season, still sits on
the league median rather than below it, which is the health-selection
wall made visual: you cannot post a very low load-based score and play a
full season, because availability is what drives the load (and the
recent-games count) the score is built from. The lowest scores in the
league belong to players barely in the rotation, so a full-season player
makes a poor low-risk exemplar.

The why lives in the same object. The score is a weighted sum, so a
player's elevation on any game decomposes into how much comes from acute
load, congestion or injury history, which is the per-player readout a
practitioner would act on.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Conclusion

Where I got to, and what carries into the article.

1.  The workload association is dominated by exposure measures. Chronic
    load (`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`) and recent games played
    (`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D")`) are the two largest workload
    terms in Model 3, and both are raised for every injury mechanism,
    the impact control included (chronic load
    `r hr(m_rep_named, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` on reported-pathology
    overuse against `r hr(m_impact, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` on impact
    injuries). That is the pattern exposure and selection would
    produce, not a fatigue gradient. Acute load adds nothing on average
    once those are held fixed (`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` in
    Model 3).

2.  An exploratory fatigue-consistent pattern, in one subset. Acute load
    is `r hr_ci_txt(m_rep_named, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` for overuse where
    a pathology is reported, not distinguishable from 1 elsewhere, and
    the difference from the control holds in a direct contrast, ratio
    `r ratio_txt(ct_rep, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`. The pre-specified
    pooled comparison does not, ratio `r ratio_txt(ct_pool, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`,
    and the split came after seeing it, so this is consistent with a
    fatigue pathway, not an identification of one.

3.  Measurement may be hiding what signal there is. Where the report
    says only that something is sore, acute load is
    `r hr(m_rep_vague, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` on
    `r format(m_rep_vague$nevent, big.mark = ",")` events. If most of
    what availability text records as overuse is precautionary rest
    written down as a symptom, surveillance built on that text will
    understate any workload association with overuse injury.

4.  Prior injury is the largest change in a player's risk profile, and
    the covariates do not carry it. Holding workload, schedule and
    context equal, a player in their second injury spell of a season
    carries `r esc2`x the baseline hazard of a player in their first and
    a third-or-later spell `r esc3`x. Because the spell strata take no
    coefficient, none of that is attributable to load; it sits in the
    baseline, where no amount of load management would show it.

5.  Load is interchangeable with minutes, and catching why mattered. I
    report load as the better construct, and the model holds identically
    on minutes. An earlier version had load out-predicting minutes for
    soft tissue (0.693 → 0.744); that was a tracking-data bug, DNP games
    leaking a fake zero distance through the carry-forward, not a real
    edge. Distance is the right idea, but in public data total load ≈
    minutes (r ≈ 0.99) and the injurious high-speed component is
    unobserved.

6.  Background risk rises across the season. Model 3's per-game
    baseline hazard is `r sprintf("%.2f", late_rate / early_rate)`x
    higher in games 55-75 than 5-25, with the post-All-Star term
    (`r hr(m3, "IS_POST_ALLSTAR")`) carrying part of the late-season rise
    as well. The workload terms show no detected change in relative
    effect across the season, so it is the baseline that moves, not how
    those terms act. It is a residual conditional on the model, and on
    its own it does not say which scheduling change would help.

7.  Proneness is real, and the covariates absorb about
    `r pct_absorbed`% of it. θ =
    `r round(theta, 3)` against `r round(theta_steps[1], 3)` unadjusted,
    so the 90th-to-10th spread narrows from
    `r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps[1])), 1)`x to
    `r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)`x. What remains is the
    reach of public data.

## Limitations

-   Health-gating is not solved. Point-in-time rest and back-to-back
    covariates read protective because coaches rest at-risk players. I
    mark them rather than interpret them; observational data cannot
    remove the bias.
-   The outcome is availability, not diagnosis. "Listed Out with a
    reason", not a clinician's assessment, and the reason text is
    inconsistent.
-   Concordance `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(m3)$concordance[1])` to
    `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(m3_ag)$concordance[1])` is the
    public-data ceiling. No GPS, no medical screening, no training load.
    Better framed as establishing that ceiling than as a competitive
    predictor.
-   The lagged terms cost coverage. First two appearances each season
    cannot be scored, so the model fits
    `r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` of
    `r format(sum(cox$event), big.mark = ",")` events. Early-season
    injury is the blind spot, and a fair price for a correctly-signed
    prospective term.
-   The deep bench adds uninformative at-risk time, but excluding on
    this season's games played would condition on the outcome.
-   Intensity is a per-game distance-per-minute average, which cannot
    resolve high-speed and acceleration efforts. Its null is evidence
    about this measure, not the construct.
-   Mechanism tiers involve judgement. Regex on free text; defensible
    but not uniquely so.
-   Five seasons, one league, two COVID-affected.

# Appendix - Robustness and sensitivity checks {#appendix}

Checks that the headline result does not depend on a modelling choice I
made. Each re-fits the reported specification with one decision changed
and reports what moves. They sit here rather than in the main sequence
because none of them changes a conclusion; the point of each is that
nothing happens.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Does the exposure choice matter?

Load and minutes are \~`r round(r_load_min, 3)` collinear, so does the
choice matter? Refitting Model 3 with minutes swapped in leaves
discrimination and the headline hazard ratios essentially unchanged.

```{r robustness-minutes, dependson="model-specs"}
m3_min <- fit_cox(m3_terms_min)   # same Model 3, minutes in place of load

robust_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Concordance", "Chronic workload HR (per SD)",
             "Acute workload HR (per SD)"),
  `Load (reported)` = c(
    round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
  `Minutes (robustness)` = c(
    round(summary(m3_min)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_28D"), hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_7D"))
)
show_tbl(robust_tab, "Robustness - on-court load vs minutes give the same answer")
```

So the exposure choice is not driving the result. I lead with load
because it is the better construct, what the body absorbed rather than
what the coach decided.

## Is the 2-games-back term its own signal?

Lag-2 carries correctly-signed load effect in the model. Two ways it
could be an illusion: it might just be re-expressing the 7d/28d rolling
windows, or its contribution might be in-sample overfitting.

```{r sensitivity-lag2, dependson="model-specs"}
load_block <- c("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")

# How much of lag-2 do the rolling windows explain? VIF < 5 = estimable alongside them.
lag2_vif <- 1 / (1 - summary(lm(z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE ~ z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D +
                   z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D, data = cox))$r.squared)

# Out of sample: refit on 2021-25, score the unseen 2025-26, with and without lag-2.
tr <- cox %>% filter(SEASON != "2025-26"); te <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == "2025-26")
oos_c <- function(terms) {           # no season strata, so the score transfers
  f <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(terms, collapse = " + "),
                               " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")), data = tr, ties = "efron")
  d <- te; d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(f, newdata = te, type = "lp"))
  round(concordance(Surv(t_start, t_stop, event) ~ .lp, data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance, 4)
}

oos_with <- oos_c(m3_terms)
oos_less <- oos_c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"))

lag2_tab <- tibble(
  Check = c("VIF of lag-2 against the rolling-load block",
            "Out-of-sample C, lag-2 in the model",
            "Out-of-sample C, lag-2 dropped"),
  Value = c(round(lag2_vif, 2),
            oos_with, oos_less))
show_tbl(lag2_tab, "Is the 2-games-back term its own signal?")
```

VIF is inside the conventional threshold of 5, so lag-2 is estimable
alongside the rolling windows. I

What justifies keeping it is the hold-out: concordance `r oos_with` with
lag-2 against `r oos_less` without. It adds predictive value on a season
the model never saw, which is the test that matters for a term I report
as a finding.

## Does intensity add anything beyond volume?

Load and minutes are both volume. Intensity is the obvious candidate for
what they miss: how hard, not how long. It is nearly uncorrelated with
the load terms, so if it carried independent signal this is where it
would show. I add the same prospective lag pair to Model 3 and test
whether both terms are jointly zero.

```{r robustness-intensity, dependson="model-specs"}
# Fit on the rows where intensity is defined for BOTH models, so the comparison is like for like (intensity needs >=10 minutes played, so it is missing more often than load).
need_int <- c(setdiff(m3_terms, "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)"), intensity_terms)
cox_int  <- cox %>% filter(if_all(all_of(need_int), ~ !is.na(.)))

m3_int_base <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                     " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_int, ties = "efron")
m3_int_plus <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ",
                     paste(c(m3_terms, intensity_terms), collapse = " + "),
                     " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_int, ties = "efron")

# Joint robust Wald test that both intensity coefficients are zero.
cf <- coef(m3_int_plus); V <- vcov(m3_int_plus); idx <- match(intensity_terms, names(cf))
int_wald <- as.numeric(t(cf[idx]) %*% solve(V[idx, idx]) %*% cf[idx])
int_p    <- pchisq(int_wald, length(idx), lower.tail = FALSE)

intensity_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Concordance", "Chronic load HR (per SD)", "Acute load HR (per SD)",
             "In-game intensity, last game (per SD)", "In-game intensity, 2 games back (per SD)"),
  `Model 3` = c(round(summary(m3_int_base)$concordance[1], 4),
                hr(m3_int_base, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_int_base, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), NA, NA),
  `+ intensity` = c(round(summary(m3_int_plus)$concordance[1], 4),
                hr(m3_int_plus, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_int_plus, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
                hr(m3_int_plus, "z_PREV_GAME_INTENSITY"), hr(m3_int_plus, "z_PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY"))
)
show_tbl(intensity_tab, paste0("Intensity robustness - joint Wald test that both intensity terms are zero: p = ",
                               fmt_p(int_p)))
```

Intensity adds nothing once volume is accounted for. Concordance
unchanged to three decimals, load hazard ratios unmoved, both intensity
terms close to 1.

These players all move at broadly similar rates, so a per-SD move in
intensity is a small physical change. This is evidence that the narrow
band of intensity visible in public tracking data carries no signal
beyond volume, not that effort is irrelevant. The high-speed and
acceleration component the literature implicates is not resolvable in a
per-game distance-per-minute average. Intensity stays out of the primary
model.

## Does the tier pattern depend on how acute load is expressed?

Acute load and recent games played are both in Model 3, and they are
strongly correlated. Holding games fixed is what lets the acute
coefficient mean load concentrated within the same number of recent
games. The obvious alternative expresses that concentration directly, as
distance per recent game, in place of total seven-day distance. If the
Stage 6 pattern (acute load raised only for overuse with a reported
pathology) is robust, it should survive that change.

```{r sensitivity-acute-form, dependson="mechanism"}
# Distance per appearance over the last 7 days (0 when no games), standardised like
# every other continuous term.
cox$LOAD_PER_GAME_7D   <- ifelse(cox$ROLLING_GAMES_7D > 0,
                                 cox$ROLLING_LOAD_7D / cox$ROLLING_GAMES_7D, 0)
cox$z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D <- as.numeric(scale(cox$LOAD_PER_GAME_7D))

rho_games_acute <- cor(cox$ROLLING_GAMES_7D, cox$ROLLING_LOAD_7D,
                       method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
# Refit Model 3 here rather than reuse the cached m3: a cached fit cannot rebuild its
# model matrix (see the note in Stage 4).
m3_now <- fit_outcome("event", m3_terms)
vif_m3 <- diag(solve(cor(model.matrix(m3_now))))

pg_terms <- c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")
pg_fits  <- list(fit_outcome("ev_rep_named", pg_terms), fit_outcome("ev_rep_vague", pg_terms),
                 fit_outcome("event_acute_nc", pg_terms), fit_outcome("event_acute_imp", pg_terms))
m3_pg    <- fit_outcome("event", pg_terms)

ct_rep_pg  <- tier_contrast("ev_rep_named",     "event_acute_imp", "reported", "impact",
                            terms = pg_terms, focus = "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")
ct_pool_pg <- tier_contrast("event_repetitive", "event_acute_imp", "overuse",  "impact",
                            terms = pg_terms, focus = "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")

acute_form_tab <- tibble(
  ` ` = c(nms, "Reported / control", "All overuse / control", "Model 3 concordance"),
  `Total 7-day distance (primary)` = c(
    map_chr(mods, ~ ci_cell(.x, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    ratio_cell(ct_rep, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), ratio_cell(ct_pool, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
    sprintf("%.3f", summary(m3)$concordance[1])),
  `Distance per recent game` = c(
    map_chr(pg_fits, ~ ci_cell(.x, "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")),
    ratio_cell(ct_rep_pg, "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D"), ratio_cell(ct_pool_pg, "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D"),
    sprintf("%.3f", summary(m3_pg)$concordance[1])))
show_tbl(acute_form_tab, paste0(
  "Acute-load term by tier under two forms (HR per SD, 95% CI; contrasts from the joint model). ",
  "Spearman correlation of games played and acute load (7d): ", sprintf("%.2f", rho_games_acute),
  "; VIF of acute load in Model 3: ", sprintf("%.1f", vif_m3[["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"]])))
```

The Stage 6 pattern does not survive the change of form. Expressed as
distance per recent game, the load term is
`r ci_cell(pg_fits[[4]], "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")` on the impact control
and `r ci_cell(pg_fits[[1]], "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")` on overuse with a
reported pathology, and the contrast between them is
`r ratio_txt(ct_rep_pg, "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")`. Discrimination is
essentially the same under either form. So the acute-load difference
between tiers depends on how acute load is expressed, which is one more
reason the tier result is reported as exploratory. The exposure terms
stay large under both forms: with the per-game form, chronic load is
`r hr(m3_pg, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` and recent games played
`r hr(m3_pg, "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D")` in Model 3, against
`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` and `r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D")` in
the primary form, and load per recent game itself is
`r hr_ci_txt(m3_pg, "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_7D")` for all new injuries.

## Does holding the 28-day game count fixed change chronic load?

Recent games played is what lets the acute term mean load concentrated
within the same number of games. The same move on the chronic side holds
the number of games in the last 28 days fixed, leaving 28-day distance at
the same game count. If that remainder were fatigue, it should be larger
for overuse than for the impact control. Two forms are tested: Model 3
with games played in the last 28 days added, and chronic load expressed
as distance per game over 28 days alongside that count.

```{r sensitivity-chronic-form, dependson="sensitivity-acute-form"}
cox$z_ROLLING_GAMES_28D <- as.numeric(scale(cox$ROLLING_GAMES_28D))
cox$LOAD_PER_GAME_28D   <- ifelse(cox$ROLLING_GAMES_28D > 0,
                                  cox$ROLLING_LOAD_28D / cox$ROLLING_GAMES_28D, 0)
cox$z_LOAD_PER_GAME_28D <- as.numeric(scale(cox$LOAD_PER_GAME_28D))

chronic_forms <- list(
  primary = list(label = "Model 3 (primary)", term = "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",
                 terms = m3_terms),
  games28 = list(label = "+ games played (28d)", term = "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",
                 terms = c(m3_terms, "z_ROLLING_GAMES_28D")),
  pergame = list(label = "Distance per game (28d) + games played (28d)", term = "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_28D",
                 terms = c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),
                           "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_28D", "z_ROLLING_GAMES_28D")))

# Every fit uses Model 3's rows, so concordance and AIC are comparable across forms.
chronic_fits <- map(chronic_forms, function(s) list(
  all   = fit_outcome("event", s$terms),
  tiers = map(c("ev_rep_named", "ev_rep_vague", "event_acute_nc", "event_acute_imp"),
              ~ fit_outcome(.x, s$terms)),
  rep   = tier_contrast("ev_rep_named",     "event_acute_imp", "reported", "impact",
                        terms = s$terms, focus = s$term),
  pool  = tier_contrast("event_repetitive", "event_acute_imp", "overuse",  "impact",
                        terms = s$terms, focus = s$term)))

chronic_form_tab <- imap_dfr(chronic_forms, function(s, k) {
  f <- chronic_fits[[k]]
  tibble(Specification = s$label,
         `All new injuries` = ci_cell(f$all, s$term),
         !!!set_names(as.list(map_chr(f$tiers, ~ ci_cell(.x, s$term))), nms),
         `Reported / control`    = ratio_cell(f$rep,  s$term),
         `All overuse / control` = ratio_cell(f$pool, s$term),
         C   = sprintf("%.3f", summary(f$all)$concordance[1]),
         AIC = sprintf("%.1f", AIC(f$all)))
})
show_tbl(chronic_form_tab, paste0(
  "Chronic-load term by tier under three forms (HR per SD, 95% CI; contrasts from the joint model). ",
  "Spearman correlation of games played (28d) and chronic load: ",
  sprintf("%.2f", cor(cox$ROLLING_GAMES_28D, cox$ROLLING_LOAD_28D, method = "spearman"))))

pg28_zph  <- cox.zph(chronic_fits$pergame$all, transform = "identity")$table["z_LOAD_PER_GAME_28D", "p"]
aic_gain  <- AIC(chronic_fits$primary$all) - AIC(chronic_fits$pergame$all)
```

Neither form makes chronic load specific to overuse. With the 28-day
game count held fixed, chronic load is
`r ci_cell(chronic_fits$games28$tiers[[4]], "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` on the
impact control against
`r ci_cell(chronic_fits$games28$tiers[[1]], "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` on
overuse with a reported pathology, a ratio of
`r ratio_txt(chronic_fits$games28$rep, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`. In the
per-game form the ratio is
`r ratio_txt(chronic_fits$pergame$rep, "z_LOAD_PER_GAME_28D")`. Distance
at a fixed number of games is mostly minutes per game (load and minutes
correlate at \~`r round(r_load_min, 3)`), so what remains is still time
on court, per game rather than in total, which is exposure. Model 3 stays
as it is.

The per-game form does fit better: concordance
`r sprintf("%.3f", summary(chronic_fits$pergame$all)$concordance[1])`
against `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(chronic_fits$primary$all)$concordance[1])`,
AIC lower by `r round(aic_gain)`, with distance per game the largest term
in the model and elevated in every tier. I found that after looking, and
its proportional-hazards test flags (p = `r fmt_p(pg28_zph)`), so it is a
lead for an exposure measure to prespecify in future work rather than a
result here.

## Does the deep bench dilute the result?

The sample is every player who appeared at all, including the very end
of the rotation: 1-to-20-game seasons, single-digit minutes. Their
availability is driven by roster politics more than health, so they add
at-risk time that is largely noise. About 23% of player-seasons and 11%
of rows, but under 5% of events, which is the profile of observations
that dilute rather than inform.

A player appears in few games precisely because he got hurt, so
filtering on current availability deletes the injured and biases the
effect toward null. That is conditioning on a post-baseline outcome.
Instead the cohort is defined ex ante on the previous season's minutes
per game, fixed before any of this season's injuries.

```{r sensitivity-rotation, dependson="model-specs"}
ROTATION_MPG <- 15   # prior-season minutes per game: an established rotation player

rot_groups <- cox %>%
  mutate(Group = case_when(
    is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG)              ~ "No prior-season record",
    PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG >= ROTATION_MPG     ~ paste0("Rotation (>= ", ROTATION_MPG, " mpg)"),
    TRUE                                    ~ paste0("Below threshold (< ", ROTATION_MPG, " mpg)"))) %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(`Intervals` = n(), Events = sum(event),
            `Events per 1,000 intervals` = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 2), .groups = "drop")
show_tbl(rot_groups, "Event rate by prior-season role (the dilution, quantified)")

rate_of  <- function(pat) rot_groups[["Events per 1,000 intervals"]][grepl(pat, rot_groups$Group)]
rate_low <- rate_of("Below"); rate_rot <- rate_of("Rotation"); rate_na <- rate_of("No prior")
n_noprior <- cox %>% distinct(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG))) %>% pull(n)

# season's injuries occur and the cohort stays ex ante.
cox <- cox %>%
  mutate(CAREER_MPG     = if_else(CAREER_GAMES > 0, CAREER_MINUTES / CAREER_GAMES, NA_real_),
         ROTATION_BASIS = coalesce(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG, CAREER_MPG))

n_restored <- cox %>% distinct(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG) & ROTATION_BASIS >= ROTATION_MPG, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pull(n)

cox_rot <- cox %>% filter(ROTATION_BASIS >= ROTATION_MPG)
m3_rot  <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                 " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_rot, ties = "efron")

rot_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Player-intervals (n)", "Events", "Concordance",
             "Chronic load HR (per SD)", "Acute load HR (per SD)",
             "In-game load, last game", "In-game load, 2 games back"),
  `All players (primary)` = c(m3$n, m3$nevent, round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
     hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
     hr(m3, "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE"), hr(m3, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")),
  `Rotation players only` = c(m3_rot$n, m3_rot$nevent, round(summary(m3_rot)$concordance[1], 4),
     hr(m3_rot, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_rot, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
     hr(m3_rot, "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE"), hr(m3_rot, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"))
)
show_tbl(rot_tab, paste0("Sensitivity - restricted to established rotation players (>= ",
                         ROTATION_MPG, " mpg in the prior season, or across their career ",
                         "where the prior season is missing)"))
```

The workload result is not an artefact of the deep bench. Restricting to
established rotation players raises the workload hazard ratios.
Discrimination goes the other way.

A more homogeneous cohort estimates the effects on a cleaner population
while leaving less variation to rank. Full sample stays primary because
it describes the league, not a subset.

Filtering on prior-season minutes alone silently deletes the
`r n_noprior` player-seasons with no prior-season record, because `NA`
fails a `>=` test. The group is Klay Thompson, Kawhi Leonard, Jamal
Murray, John Wall, Zion Williamson, all of whom missed a full season
through injury. Dropping the highest injury-burden players in the league
on a this would bias the check in the one direction . Where the prior
season is missing I fall back to career minutes per game, restoring
`r n_restored` player-seasons. Career totals use only seasons before the
modelled one, so the cohort stays ex ante.

I keep the full sample as primary (it is the honest population of NBA
players and the broader claim) Rookies sit outside this check by
construction: no prior season, no career history to fall back on.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Does the choice of time scale matter?

Everything above runs on one time axis: the player's position through
their team's scheduled games. That is a modelling decision, not a fact
about the data, and it usually goes unexamined. So I tested the
alternative.

The competing clock counts a player's at-risk intervals, closing the
gaps injury absences leave. LeBron's first 2025-26 appearance is game 15
on the scheduled clock and game 1 on this one. Not cosmetic: it changes
who sits in the same risk set. Scheduled compares players at the same
point in the season, at-risk compares them at the same number of
available games.

```{r clock-robustness, dependson=c("m3","mechanism")}
cox_b <- cox %>% arrange(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, t_stop) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID) %>%
  mutate(b_stop = row_number(), b_start = b_stop - 1L) %>% ungroup()
stopifnot(all(cox_b$b_stop > cox_b$b_start))

fit_b <- function(outcome, terms = m3_terms) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(b_start, b_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ ",
        paste(terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail)),
        data = cox_b, ties = "efron")
}
m3_b     <- fit_b("event")
msoft_b  <- fit_b("event_repetitive"); mload_b <- fit_b("event_acute_nc")
mimp_b   <- fit_b("event_acute_imp")

clock_tab <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Model 3: chronic load (28d)", "Model 3: acute load (7d)",
               "Model 3: concordance",
               "Repetitive: chronic / acute", "Acute non-contact: chronic / acute",
               "Acute impact: chronic / acute"),
  `Scheduled-game clock` = c(
    hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
    round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
    paste(hr(m_soft,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(m_soft,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(m_load,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(m_load,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(m_impact,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),"/", hr(m_impact,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))),
  `At-risk-interval clock` = c(
    hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
    round(summary(m3_b)$concordance[1], 4),
    paste(hr(msoft_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), "/", hr(msoft_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(mload_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), "/", hr(mload_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(mimp_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(mimp_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))))

# How far apart are the two clocks in the first place?
clock_gap <- cox_b %>% summarise(
  `Rows where the clocks agree` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*mean(t_stop == b_stop)),
  `Mean absolute difference`    = round(mean(abs(t_stop - b_stop)), 2),
  `Largest difference`          = max(abs(t_stop - b_stop)))

show_tbl(clock_tab, "Time-scale robustness: scheduled-game clock vs at-risk-interval clock")
show_tbl(clock_gap, "How far apart the two clocks actually are")
```

## What it shows

Nothing moves. Chronic load `r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` to
`r hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`, acute load
`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` to `r hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`,
concordance `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4)` to
`r round(summary(m3_b)$concordance[1], 4)`. The tier estimates move
just as little: acute load on the control is
`r hr(mimp_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` on this clock against
`r hr(m_impact, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` on the scheduled clock, and chronic
load on the control `r hr(mimp_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` against
`r hr(m_impact, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`.

I had expected chronic load to fall, on the reasoning that a clock
counting available games would absorb some of the exposure signal. It
does not. The clocks agree on
`r clock_gap[["Rows where the clocks agree"]]` of rows and differ by
`r clock_gap[["Mean absolute difference"]]` games on average, so
absences are not frequent enough to reshape the risk sets. Season
progress moves, but that is redistribution.

Scheduled clock stays primary. It is the axis where the baseline hazard
has a season interpretation (Stage 6), and the one that puts players at
the same position in their team's schedule in the same risk set, which
approximates the comparison a team makes. The estimates do not depend on it, which is the
useful part.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Article export {.unnumbered}

Everything the journal article uses is written out from here, so the
article can never drift from this report. Figures go to `docs/figures/`
at print resolution, tables to `docs/tables/` as CSV. Re-knitting
regenerates all of them.

```{r article-export, dependson=c("risk-set-schematic","calibration-plot","trajectory","risk-profiles","hr-table","recurrent-compare","mechanism","player-cv","sensitivity-rotation","robustness-intensity","robustness-minutes","ph-decomp","stage0-screening","nested-tests","oos-calibration","ag-model")}
FIG <- here("docs", "figures"); TAB <- here("docs", "tables")
dir.create(FIG, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(TAB, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Print styling: larger base type than the screen version, because these land in a
# Word document at roughly half the on-screen width.
print_theme <- theme(text = element_text(size = 13),
                     plot.title = element_blank(),      # the article caption carries the title
                     plot.subtitle = element_blank())

save_fig <- function(plot, name, w, h) {
  ggsave(file.path(FIG, paste0(name, ".png")), plot + print_theme,
         width = w, height = h, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
  invisible(name)
}

save_fig(fig_riskset,  "figure1_risk_set_schematic", 10.0, 4.6)
save_fig(fig_calib,    "figure2_calibration_decile",  7.0, 4.5)
save_fig(fig_traj,     "figure3_baseline_hazard",     7.5, 4.5)
save_fig(fig_profiles, "figure4_rolling_profiles",    8.0, 8.5)

# Appendix B1: all 25 scaled-Schoenfeld curves on one sheet. cox.zph plots are base
# graphics, so this is drawn straight to a device rather than through ggsave.
png(file.path(FIG, "appendixB1_schoenfeld_panel.png"),
    width = 10, height = 12.5, units = "in", res = 200)
op <- par(mfrow = c(7, 4), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 2.0, 0.8), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.62)
for (v in plot_terms) {
  idx <- which(rownames(zph3$table) == v)
  plot(zph3[idx], resid = FALSE, lwd = 1.6, col = "steelblue",
       main = sub("^z_", "", v), xlab = "Game number", ylab = "beta(t)")
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey55", lty = 2)
}
par(op); invisible(dev.off())

# Tables. Each is written exactly as the article reports it, so the article can be

write_tab <- function(x, name) {

}

# Presentation export {.unnumbered}

Slide versions of the figures: fewer elements, much larger type, and one
new figure that the article does not need. The negative control is a
table in the article, but it is the centre of the talk, so it gets a
purpose-built chart here. Everything writes to
`docs/figures/presentation/`.

```{r presentation-export, dependson=c("m3","mechanism","calibration-plot","trajectory","risk-profiles","frailty-nested","risk-set-schematic")}
PFIG <- here("docs", "figures", "presentation")
dir.create(PFIG, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

pres_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 19) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 21),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15, colour = "grey30"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 16),
        legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 15))

psave <- function(pl, name, w = 11, h = 6.2)
  ggsave(file.path(PFIG, paste0(name, ".png")), pl, width = w, height = h,
         dpi = 200, bg = "white")

## P1 - chronic and acute load across the four tiers, the same model fitted to each.
## Titles are descriptive on purpose: what the pattern means belongs on the slide, where
## it can be worded as exploratory, not baked into an image that outlives a rerun.
## Point estimates are plotted and significance is marked, because the reading needs both.
tier_lv <- c("Overuse\n(pathology reported)", "Overuse\n(symptom only)",
             "Acute\nnon-contact", "Acute impact\n(CONTROL)")
p1_mods <- list(m_rep_named, m_rep_vague, m_load, m_impact)

pull_hr <- function(term) map_dbl(p1_mods, ~ hr(.x, term))
pull_p  <- function(term) map_dbl(p1_mods, ~ summary(.x)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|z|)"])
# 95% CI from each tier's robust (player-clustered) covariance, as in Table 4
pull_ci <- function(term, z) map_dbl(p1_mods, ~ exp(coef(.x)[[term]] + z * sqrt(vcov(.x)[term, term])))

neg <- tibble(
  tier = factor(rep(tier_lv, 2), levels = tier_lv),
  what = rep(c("Chronic load (28d)", "Acute load (7d)"), each = 4),
  hr   = c(pull_hr("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), pull_hr("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
  lo   = c(pull_ci("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", -1.96), pull_ci("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", -1.96)),
  hi   = c(pull_ci("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",  1.96), pull_ci("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",  1.96)),
  p    = c(pull_p("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  pull_p("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))) %>%
  mutate(sig   = p < 0.05,
         # label carries the estimate; "ns" flags the ones you cannot distinguish from 1
         label = ifelse(sig, sprintf("%.2f", hr), sprintf("%.2f\nns", hr)),
         # the two series sit either side of the tier, so their intervals never overlap
         # (in the first tier they cover almost the same range). P1a uses the same offset,
         # so the build from one slide to the next does not jump.
         x = as.numeric(tier) + ifelse(what == "Chronic load (28d)", -0.07, 0.07))

# Shared by P1 and P1a. The intervals are drawn faint and first, so on a projector the
# points and lines still carry the slide, while anyone reading closely can see the CIs.
# Labels sit on a white patch so a CI passing behind them does not cut the number.
neg_layers <- function(d) list(
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55", linewidth = .7),
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = .06, linewidth = 1.1, alpha = .28,
                show.legend = FALSE),
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.6),
  # hollow points = not distinguishable from no effect, solid = significant
  geom_point(aes(shape = sig, fill = what), size = 5.5, stroke = 1.6),
  # chronic labels above their points, acute labels below: where the two estimates are
  # close (the first tier) a shared position put one label on top of the other point
  geom_label(aes(label = label, vjust = ifelse(what == "Acute load (7d)", 1.45, -0.6)),
             size = 5.2, fontface = "bold", lineheight = .85, fill = "white",
             label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(.12, "lines"), show.legend = FALSE),
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 2.86, label = "least plausibly load-driven",
           size = 4.6, colour = "grey25", fontface = "italic"),
  annotate("segment", x = 3.72, xend = 4.28, y = 2.76, yend = 2.76,
           colour = "grey35", linewidth = .5),
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = tier_lv, limits = c(0.5, 4.5), expand = c(0, 0)),
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 21, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none"),
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.3, 2.95), breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5)),
  labs(subtitle = paste0("Hazard ratio per SD, the same model fitted to each tier.\n",
                         "Faint bars: 95% CI. Hollow points: CI includes 1."),
       x = NULL, y = "Hazard ratio"),
  pres_theme)

p_neg <- ggplot(neg, aes(x, hr, colour = what, group = what)) +
  neg_layers() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Chronic load (28d)" = "#2166AC", "Acute load (7d)" = "#B2182B")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Chronic load (28d)" = "#2166AC", "Acute load (7d)" = "#B2182B"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Workload hazard ratios by injury mechanism")
psave(p_neg, "P1_negative_control")

## P1a - the same axes carrying the chronic series alone, so a talk can show chronic
## load first and add the acute series on the next slide. Same scales as P1, so the
## second slide reads as the first with a line added.
p_neg1 <- ggplot(filter(neg, what == "Chronic load (28d)"),
                 aes(x, hr, colour = what, group = what)) +
  neg_layers() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Chronic load (28d)" = "#2166AC")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Chronic load (28d)" = "#2166AC"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Chronic load by injury mechanism")
psave(p_neg1, "P1a_chronic_only")

## P2 - calibration, simplified
p_cal <- ggplot(calib, aes(risk_group, event_rate_1k)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", width = .68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(event_rate_1k)), vjust = -0.5, size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(title = "Higher risk score, more injuries",
       subtitle = "Observed injury rate by predicted-risk decile. Every step rises.",
       x = "Risk decile (1 = lowest)", y = "Injuries per 1,000 games") +
  pres_theme
psave(p_cal, "P2_calibration")

## P3 - baseline hazard, with the arithmetic behind the ratio drawn on the curve. The
## slope of a cumulative hazard is the hazard per game, so each window gets a
## rise-over-run triangle: across 20 games, then up by the hazard added over them.
win <- tibble(g0 = c(5, 55), g1 = c(25, 75)) %>%
  mutate(h0 = map_dbl(g0, haz_at), h1 = map_dbl(g1, haz_at),
         rise = h1 - h0, per_k = 1000 * rise / 20,
         lab = sprintf("Games %d–%d\nrises %.2f over 20 games\n= %.1f per 1,000 games",
                       g0, g1, rise, per_k))
ratio_lab <- sprintf("%.1f ÷ %.1f = %.1fx steeper\nlate in the season",
                     win$per_k[2], win$per_k[1], win$per_k[2] / win$per_k[1])
y_top <- max(traj$cum_haz)

p_traj <- ggplot(traj, aes(game_number, cum_haz)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = win$g0, xmax = win$g1, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey50", alpha = .09) +
  geom_segment(data = win, aes(x = g0, xend = g1, y = h0, yend = h0), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               colour = "grey30", linewidth = .9, linetype = "22") +
  geom_segment(data = win, aes(x = g1, xend = g1, y = h0, yend = h1), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               colour = "grey30", linewidth = .9, linetype = "22") +
  geom_line(colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 1.7) +
  geom_point(data = win, aes(x = g0, y = h0), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#B2182B", size = 3.2) +
  geom_point(data = win, aes(x = g1, y = h1), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#B2182B", size = 3.2) +
  # early window labelled above the curve, late window below it: both sit in empty space
  annotate("text", x = win$g0[1], y = win$h1[1] + 0.2 * y_top, label = win$lab[1],
           hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 5, lineheight = .95, colour = "grey20") +
  annotate("text", x = win$g0[2], y = win$h0[2] - 0.12 * y_top, label = win$lab[2],
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 5, lineheight = .95, colour = "grey20") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = y_top, label = ratio_lab, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 6.6, fontface = "bold", lineheight = .95, colour = "#B2182B") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 20, 40, 60, 80)) +
  labs(title = "Baseline injury risk rises through the season",
       subtitle = paste0("A steeper curve means a higher injury hazard per game. ",
                         "Player at the reference level of every covariate."),
       x = "Game number", y = "Cumulative baseline hazard") +
  pres_theme
psave(p_traj, "P3_baseline_hazard")

## P4 - frailty progression: the spread the covariates absorb
fr <- tibble(step = factor(c("No covariates", "+ Workload", "+ Schedule", "+ Player context"),
                           levels = c("No covariates", "+ Workload", "+ Schedule", "+ Player context")),
             spread = exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps)))
p_fr <- ggplot(fr, aes(step, spread)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", width = .66) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1fx", spread)), vjust = -0.45, size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .15))) +
  labs(title = "The model explains two thirds of what separates players",
       subtitle = "Spread in injury proneness, 90th vs 10th percentile, as covariates are added",
       x = NULL, y = "Hazard spread") +
  pres_theme
psave(p_fr, "P4_frailty_progression")

## P5 - rolling profiles, larger type
psave(fig_profiles + theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
        theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 14),
              plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 20)),
      "P5_rolling_profiles", w = 10.5, h = 7.4)

## P6 - risk-set schematic, larger type
psave(fig_riskset + theme(text = element_text(size = 15),
                          legend.text = element_text(size = 12)),
      "P6_risk_set", w = 12, h = 5.6)

## P7 - what "per SD of chronic load" means, for the headline slide. A per-SD hazard
## ratio is hard to follow when said aloud, so the slide shows where players actually sit
## on 28-day distance and how far one SD reaches in basketball terms (P7a), then what
## that gap does to risk for the same player with the same games this week (P7b).
modelled    <- cox %>% filter(!is.na(z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE))     # the rows Model 3 uses
sd_chronic  <- sd(cox$ROLLING_LOAD_28D, na.rm = TRUE)             # the SD the z-score used
mi_per_game <- mean(cox$DISTANCE[cox$PLAYED_FLAG == 1 & cox$DISTANCE > 0], na.rm = TRUE)

# Role from the player's minutes per game played that season (descriptive only).
role_of <- cox %>% filter(PLAYED_FLAG == 1) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID) %>%
  summarise(mpg = mean(as.numeric(MIN), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(role = cut(mpg, c(-Inf, 15, 28, Inf),
                    labels = c("Bench", "Rotation", "Starter")))
roles <- modelled %>% inner_join(role_of, by = c("SEASON", "PLAYER_ID")) %>%
  group_by(role) %>%
  summarise(miles = median(ROLLING_LOAD_28D), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(sub = c("under 15 min a game", "15 to 28 min", "28+ min"))

bins  <- modelled %>% mutate(bin = 2 * floor(ROLLING_LOAD_28D / 2)) %>% count(bin) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
y_top <- max(bins$share)
rot   <- roles$miles[roles$role == "Rotation"]
br_y  <- 1.18 * y_top                                     # bracket height
lab_y <- 1.42 * y_top                                     # role labels sit above it

p_sd_a <- ggplot(bins, aes(bin + 1, share)) +
  geom_col(width = 1.9, fill = "#2166AC", alpha = .22) +
  geom_segment(data = roles, aes(x = miles, xend = miles, y = 0, yend = 1.32 * y_top),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#2166AC", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = roles, aes(x = miles, y = lab_y, label = paste0(role, "\n", round(miles), " miles")),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#2166AC", fontface = "bold", size = 5.2, lineheight = .9) +
  # one SD drawn to scale, starting at the rotation median
  annotate("segment", x = rot, xend = rot + sd_chronic, y = br_y, yend = br_y,
           colour = "grey20", linewidth = 1.1,
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", angle = 90, length = unit(.12, "inches"))) +
  annotate("label", x = rot + sd_chronic / 2, y = br_y,
           label = sprintf("1 SD = %.0f miles\n≈ %.0f games of running", sd_chronic, sd_chronic / mi_per_game),
           size = 4.8, fontface = "bold", lineheight = .9, fill = "white", label.size = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, 10), expand = expansion(mult = c(.01, .02))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1.55 * y_top),
                     breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(3)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, quantile(modelled$ROLLING_LOAD_28D, .995))) +
  labs(title = "Where players sit on chronic load",
       subtitle = "Distance covered in games over the previous 28 days, every modelled player-game.\nLines: the median for each role, by minutes per game that season.",
       x = "Miles covered in the previous 28 days", y = "Share of player-games") +
  pres_theme

b_c  <- coef(m3)[["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"]]
se_c <- sqrt(vcov(m3)["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"])
sd_bars <- tibble(
  who = factor(c("Reference\nplayer", sprintf("+%.0f miles over\nthe past 4 weeks", sd_chronic)),
               levels = c("Reference\nplayer", sprintf("+%.0f miles over\nthe past 4 weeks", sd_chronic))),
  hr = c(1, exp(b_c)), lo = c(NA, exp(b_c - 1.96 * se_c)), hi = c(NA, exp(b_c + 1.96 * se_c)),
  fill = c("ref", "plus"))

p_sd_b <- ggplot(sd_bars, aes(who, hr, fill = fill)) +
  geom_col(width = .58) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = .1, linewidth = .9, colour = "grey25", na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(aes(y = coalesce(hi, hr), label = sprintf("%.1fx", hr)), vjust = -0.55,
            size = 7.5, fontface = "bold", colour = "grey15") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55", linewidth = .7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(ref = "grey72", plus = "#2166AC"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 2.75), breaks = c(0, 1, 2), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  labs(title = "What that gap does to injury risk",
       subtitle = "Same team, same games this week.\nHazard per game vs the reference, with 95% CI.",
       x = NULL, y = "Relative injury hazard per game") +
  pres_theme + theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

psave(p_sd_a, "P7a_chronic_load_where_players_sit", w = 11, h = 6.2)
psave(p_sd_b, "P7b_chronic_load_what_one_sd_does", w = 6.8, h = 6.2)
psave(patchwork::wrap_plots(p_sd_a, p_sd_b, widths = c(1.75, 1)), "P7_chronic_load_explained",
      w = 17, h = 6.4)

## P8 - the proneness spread as injury counts, for the frailty slide. "12-fold, 90th vs
## 10th percentile of frailty" is hard to picture, so the slide shows how many injuries
## the injury-prone player picks up for every one a durable player does, before and after
## adjustment. The per-season figures translate the unadjusted spread using the overall
## onset rate in the frailty data (every onset, the outcome the frailty model uses), and
## assume a player at risk every game, so they are illustrations, not predictions.
spread_fr <- exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps))       # 90th vs 10th percentile
n_raw <- round(spread_fr[[1]]); n_adj <- round(spread_fr[[length(spread_fr)]])
r_on  <- sum(d_f$event_recurrent) / nrow(d_f)
med_on <- r_on / exp(theta_steps[[1]] / 2)                  # median frailty, not the mean
per_season_hi <- 82 * med_on * exp(qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps[[1]]))
seasons_lo    <- 1 / (82 * med_on / exp(qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps[[1]])))

rows_fr <- tibble(
  y   = c(4.3, 3.6, 1.4, 0.7),
  who = c("Durable player", "Injury-prone player", "Durable player", "Injury-prone player"),
  n   = c(1, n_raw, 1, n_adj))
dots_fr <- rows_fr %>% rowwise() %>% reframe(y = y, x = seq_len(n))

p_fr2 <- ggplot() +
  annotate("text", x = -6.2, y = c(5.05, 2.15), hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", size = 6.2,
           label = c("Before accounting for anything",
                     "Same workload, schedule and injury history")) +
  geom_text(data = rows_fr, aes(x = -6.2, y = y, label = who), hjust = 0, size = 5.6,
            colour = "grey25") +
  geom_point(data = dots_fr, aes(x, y), shape = 21, size = 7.5, stroke = 0,
             fill = "#B2182B") +
  annotate("text", x = 1 - 0.3, y = 3.0, hjust = 0, size = 4.8, colour = "grey35",
           fontface = "italic",
           label = sprintf("Roughly one injury every %.0f seasons, against about %.0f a season",
                           seasons_lo, per_season_hi)) +
  annotate("text", x = 15.2, y = c(3.95, 1.05), label = sprintf("%dx", c(n_raw, n_adj)),
           size = 13, fontface = "bold", colour = "#B2182B") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-6.3, 16.3), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.3, 5.4)) +
  labs(title = "How much more often injury-prone players get hurt",
       subtitle = paste0("Injuries for every one a durable player picks up. Durable: more durable than ",
                         "9 in 10 players.\nInjury-prone: more injury-prone than 9 in 10 players.")) +
  pres_theme +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
psave(p_fr2, "P8_proneness_spread", w = 11, h = 6.2)

tibble(File = list.files(PFIG, pattern = "\\.png$")) %>%
  show_tbl("Slide figures written")
```

# References {.unnumbered}

Compiled for review: verify each entry's details before the final
reference list. Grouped by role, with a note on where each is used.

Statistical methodology

1.  Therneau TM, Grambsch PM. Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox
    Model. New York: Springer; 2000. The counting-process Cox framework
    and time-varying covariates (whole pipeline).
2.  Andersen PK, Gill RD. Cox's regression model for counting processes:
    a large sample study. Annals of Statistics. 1982;10(4):1100–1120.
    The Andersen–Gill recurrent-events model (Stage 4).
3.  Prentice RL, Williams BJ, Peterson AV. On the regression analysis of
    multivariate failure time data. Biometrika. 1981;68(2):373–379. The
    PWP gap-time model (Stage 4).
4.  Grambsch PM, Therneau TM. Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics
    based on weighted residuals. Biometrika. 1994;81(3):515–526. The
    scaled-Schoenfeld PH test behind `cox.zph` (Stage 2).
5.  Harrell FE Jr, Califf RM, Pryor DB, Lee KL, Rosati RA. Evaluating
    the yield of medical tests. JAMA. 1982;247(18):2543–2546. The
    concordance index (Harrell's C), used throughout for discrimination.
6.  Lipsitch M, Tchetgen Tchetgen E, Cohen T. Negative controls: a tool
    for detecting confounding and bias in observational studies.
    Epidemiology. 2010;21(3):383-388. The framework for the Stage 5
    mechanism split: the definition of a negative-control outcome, the
    conditions under which one is informative, and the reading that a
    control which fires has detected confounding rather than failed.
7.  Efron B. The efficiency of Cox's likelihood function for censored
    data. Journal of the American Statistical Association.
    1977;72(359):557–565. The Efron approximation for tied event times
    (`ties = "efron"`).

Injury classification and outcome definition

8.  Bahr R, Clarsen B, Derman W, et al. International Olympic Committee
    consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of
    epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020 (including
    the STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance,
    STROBE-SIIS). British Journal of Sports Medicine.
    2020;54(7):372-389. The framework for classifying injuries on
    independent axes (body region, tissue type, mechanism, severity),
    the acute / repetitive / mixed mechanism categories behind the Stage
    5 tiers, and the time-loss severity bands.
9.  Toohey LA, Drew MK, Fortington LV, Finch CF, Cook JL. An updated
    subsequent injury categorisation model (SIC-2.0): data-driven
    categorisation of subsequent injuries in sport. Sports Medicine.
    2018;48(9):2199-2210. The data-driven categories used to classify
    subsequent injuries on site, nature and side with no clinical input,
    which is why this model rather than a recovery-based definition.
10. Finch CF, Cook J. Categorising sports injuries in epidemiological
    studies: the subsequent injury categorisation (SIC) model to address
    multiple, recurrent and exacerbation of injuries. British Journal of
    Sports Medicine. 2014;48(17):1276-1280. The original SIC model that
    SIC-2.0 extends.
11. Fuller CW, Ekstrand J, Junge A, et al. Consensus statement on injury
    definitions and data collection procedures in studies of football
    (soccer) injuries. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in
    Sports. 2006;16(2):83-92. The basis for counting a same-site injury
    after a return to play as a recurrent injury rather than a
    continuation of the previous one, which is why my rule merges only
    repeats arriving before a durable return.
12. Heiderscheit BC, Sherry MA, Silder A, Chumanov ES, Thelen DG.
    Hamstring strain injuries: recommendations for diagnosis,
    rehabilitation, and injury prevention. Journal of Orthopaedic &
    Sports Physical Therapy. 2010;40(2):67-81. Source of the roughly
    two-week post-return window used to set the durability threshold:
    about a third of hamstring injuries recur, with the greatest risk in
    the initial two weeks after return to sport, attributed to
    inadequate rehabilitation or a premature return.
13. Eftekhari A, Cogan C, Pandya N, Feeley B. Hamstring injury
    epidemiology in the National Basketball Association over a five-year
    period. Muscles, Ligaments and Tendons Journal. 2022;12(2).
    Basketball-specific evidence on repeat injury: 81.4% of NBA players
    with a hamstring injury sustained a subsequent injury in the same
    and/or following season, and those repeats are counted as subsequent
    injuries rather than merged.
14. Green B, Schache AG, Pizzari T. What is a recurrence? The onset,
    frequency and time loss impact of recurrent calf muscle strain
    injuries in elite male Australian football players over a decade.
    BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2025;11(3):e002865. Applies the
    IOC recurrence/exacerbation distinction to a decade of surveillance
    data and documents how much subsequent-injury definitions vary
    between studies.
15. Orchard JW, Meeuwisse W, Derman W, et al. Sport Medicine Diagnostic
    Coding System (SMDCS) and the Orchard Sports Injury and Illness
    Classification System (OSIICS): revised 2020 consensus versions.
    British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;54(7):397-401. The coding
    systems that operationalise the IOC axes as body-part plus pathology
    codes; my parsed site and tissue fields follow the same split.

Applied / domain

16. Russell JL, McLean BD, Impellizzeri FM, Strack DS, Coutts AJ.
    Measuring physical demands in basketball: an explorative systematic
    review of practices. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(1):81–112. Justifies
    the on-court external-load (tracking-distance) exposure. (A review
    of load-monitoring methods; it does not support an experience/tenure
    inverted-U, so it is no longer cited for the `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²`
    term.)
17. Chan C-C, Yung PS-H, Mok K-M. The relationship between training load
    and injury risk in basketball: a systematic review. Healthcare.
    2024;12(18):1829. The training-load–injury evidence base, including
    U-shaped load–risk findings (motivates the load block).
18. Martin [author initials / journal to verify] et al. Rookie-season
    injury and career longevity in NBA players. 2021. Durability /
    injury-proneness (frailty stage, and the durability side of the
    `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²` term).
19. Hägglund M, Waldén M, Ekstrand J. Previous injury as a risk factor
    for injury in elite football: a prospective study over two
    consecutive seasons. British Journal of Sports Medicine.
    2006;40(9):767–772. Prior injury as a risk factor (the prior-episode
    and recent-return covariates).

Tenure / age: the non-linear `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²` term

20. National Basketball Association. Player Participation Policy.
    Approved by the NBA Board of Governors, September 2023. The
    institutional mechanism: pre-approved back-to-back rest for players
    aged 35+, or with roughly 34,000 career regular-season minutes or
    1,000 career games, or a serious injury history. Younger players
    receive no equivalent allowance, so acute load differs
    systematically by tenure. (Formalised from 2023-24; the same
    veteran-rest pattern existed informally earlier in the study window.
    Note the CBA's "Years of Service" provisions govern contracts and
    salary, not rest, so the Participation Policy, not the CBA, is the
    correct citation here.)
21. Morikawa LH, Tummala SV, Brinkman JC, Buckner Petty SA, Chhabra A.
    Effect of a condensed NBA season on injury risk: an analysis of the
    2020 season and player safety. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports
    Medicine. 2022;10(9). Older players showed disproportionately larger
    injury increases under schedule compression.
22. Drakos MC, Domb B, Starkey C, Callahan L, Allen AA. Injury in the
    National Basketball Association: a 17-year overview. Sports Health.
    2010;2(4):284–290. Early NBA epidemiology found no clean linear
    age-injury association, supporting a non-linear specification.
